Pilar 8 — Neural Operators over Depth-Function Space

Hugo Rodrigues

Source: vignettes/pilar8-neural-operators.Rmd
pilar8-neural-operators.Rmd

Abstract

Digital Soil Mapping predicts a soil property at a point: a depth, a location, a value. But a soil profile is not a stack of independent points — it is a function of depth, and pedogenesis is the operator that produced it. Pillar 8 learns that operator directly.

Instead of fitting ŷ=f(𝐱,z)\hat{y} = f(\mathbf{x}, z) pointwise, a neural operator learns a map between function spaces (Kovachki et al. 2023; Li et al. 2021; Lu et al. 2021),

𝒢:u↦y,u,y∈𝒞([zmin,zmax]), \mathcal{G} : u \longmapsto y, \qquad u, y \in \mathcal{C}([z_{\min}, z_{\max}]),

so that a single trained model evaluates the whole profile at once, and — this is the property that matters — can be queried at depths that were never in the training grid.

1. Why “operator” is not a synonym for “regression”

A pointwise regressor takes (𝐱,z)(\mathbf{x}, z) and returns a scalar. It has no notion that the values at z=10z = 10 cm and z=15z = 15 cm belong to the same profile, and nothing stops it from returning a physically absurd non-monotone carbon profile. Depth is just another column.

An operator learner takes the whole input function and returns the whole output function. Continuity in depth is built into the representation rather than hoped for in the output. Two constructions dominate the literature, and edaphos implements both.

1.1 Fourier Neural Operator

The FNO (Li et al. 2021) builds each layer around a convolution performed in the spectral domain. For a hidden function v(z)v(z),

(𝒦v)(z)=ℱ−1(Rθ⋅ℱv)(z), (\mathcal{K}v)(z) \;=\; \mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\big(R_\theta \cdot \mathcal{F}v\big)(z),

where ℱ\mathcal{F} is the discrete Fourier transform along depth and RθR_\theta is a learned complex multiplier applied to the lowest n_modes frequencies. Truncating the spectrum is not a computational shortcut — it is the inductive bias. It says the depth operator is smooth, which is exactly what a diffusion-and-transport account of pedogenesis implies.

Because the multiplier acts on frequencies rather than grid indices, the learned weights are independent of the discretisation — the property that makes FNO attractive in the PDE literature. Note that the edaphos implementation nonetheless evaluates on the training depth grid: predict() for an edaphos_no_fno takes covariates only. Off-grid querying is available through the DeepONet fitter (§1.2, §6), whose trunk network accepts an arbitrary depth.

1.2 DeepONet

DeepONet (Lu et al. 2021) factorises the operator into two networks:

𝒢(u)(z)≈∑k=1pbk(u)⏟branchtk(z)⏟trunk. \mathcal{G}(u)(z) \;\approx\; \sum_{k=1}^{p} \underbrace{b_k(u)}_{\text{branch}} \; \underbrace{t_k(z)}_{\text{trunk}} .

The branch reads the input function (here, the site covariates) and the trunk reads the query depth; the prediction is their inner product. This is not an arbitrary architecture — it is the constructive form of the Chen and Chen (1995) universal operator approximation theorem (Chen and Chen 1995), which guarantees that a sum of such products can approximate any continuous operator to arbitrary accuracy.

The practical consequence is the same as for the FNO, by a different route: the trunk accepts any zz, so the profile can be evaluated off-grid.

2. A dataset with a known operator

To judge whether an operator was learned we need a problem whose operator we know. Pillar 2 supplies one: the parametric pedogenetic ODE,

dydz=−λ0e−μz(y−y∞), \frac{dy}{dz} \;=\; -\lambda_0 e^{-\mu z}\,\big(y - y_\infty\big),

whose closed-form solution is

y(z)=y∞+(y0−y∞)exp⁡(−λ0μ(1−e−μz)). y(z) \;=\; y_\infty + (y_0 - y_\infty)\, \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{\lambda_0}{\mu}\big(1 - e^{-\mu z}\big)\right).

We let the four parameters depend on site covariates. The true operator is then “covariates ↦\mapsto profile”, and it is analytic, so any failure to recover it is the model’s, not the data’s.

set.seed(11)

n_sites  <- 160L
depths   <- seq(2.5, 150, length.out = 24L)     # cm

cov_mat <- cbind(
  clay   = stats::runif(n_sites, 0.10, 0.60),
  map    = stats::runif(n_sites, 0.80, 1.60),   # scaled rainfall
  relief = stats::runif(n_sites, 0.00, 1.00)
)

profile_of <- function(p, z) {
  y0     <- 20 + 25 * p[["clay"]]
  yinf   <-  2 +  6 * p[["map"]]
  lam0   <- 0.05 + 0.04 * p[["relief"]]
  mu     <- 0.02 + 0.01 * p[["clay"]]
  yinf + (y0 - yinf) * exp(-(lam0 / mu) * (1 - exp(-mu * z)))
}

targets <- t(apply(cov_mat, 1L, profile_of, z = depths))
targets <- targets + matrix(stats::rnorm(length(targets), 0, 0.25),
                            nrow(targets), ncol(targets))

dim(targets)          # sites x depths
#> [1] 160  24
round(targets[1, 1:6], 2)
#> [1] 23.56 19.00 15.61 14.22 12.76 12.25

Train/test split by site, never by depth — splitting within a profile would leak the answer.

train_id <- sample(n_sites, 120L)
test_id  <- setdiff(seq_len(n_sites), train_id)

y_tr <- targets[train_id, , drop = FALSE]; x_tr <- cov_mat[train_id, , drop = FALSE]
y_te <- targets[test_id,  , drop = FALSE]; x_te <- cov_mat[test_id,  , drop = FALSE]

3. DeepONet

no_deeponet_fit() takes the covariate matrix directly: one row per site, and the depth grid separately.

don <- no_deeponet_fit(
  depths        = depths,
  targets       = y_tr,
  covariates    = x_tr,
  backend       = "r",   # reference path; knits without libtorch
  branch_hidden = 24L,
  trunk_hidden  = 24L,
  output_dim    = 10L,
  epochs        = 400L,
  lr            = 0.02,
  seed          = 1L
)
#> [no_deeponet_fit] backend = 'r' freezes the branch/trunk hidden layers and trains a random-feature readout; use backend = 'torch' (the default when libtorch is present) to train the full DeepONet.

pred_don <- predict(don, x_te)
dim(pred_don)
#> [1] 40 24

4. Fourier Neural Operator

The FNO consumes a depth-resolved covariate cube (sites, depths, channels). Static site covariates are broadcast along the depth axis:

cube <- function(x) {
  a <- array(0, dim = c(nrow(x), length(depths), ncol(x)))
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(x))) a[, , j] <- x[, j]
  a
}

fno <- no_fno_fit(
  depths     = depths,
  targets    = y_tr,
  covariates = cube(x_tr),
  backend    = "r",   # reference path; knits without libtorch
  n_modes    = 6L,
  width      = 8L,
  n_blocks   = 1L,
  epochs     = 60L,
  lr         = 0.01,
  seed       = 1L
)
#> [no_fno_fit] backend = 'r' is a frozen-spectral random-feature reference and does NOT learn the operator; use backend = 'torch' (the default when libtorch is present) for the trained Fourier Neural Operator.

pred_fno <- predict(fno, cube(x_te))
dim(pred_fno)
#> [1] 40 24

5. Scoring, against a baseline that is not a straw man

An operator model should be compared with the honest pointwise alternative: flatten every (site, depth) pair into a row, hand a random forest the depth as an extra feature, and let it compete.

flatten <- function(x, y) {
  data.frame(
    z    = rep(depths, each = nrow(x)),
    clay = rep(x[, "clay"],   times = length(depths)),
    map  = rep(x[, "map"],    times = length(depths)),
    rel  = rep(x[, "relief"], times = length(depths)),
    y    = as.vector(y)
  )
}

d_tr <- flatten(x_tr, y_tr)
d_te <- flatten(x_te, y_te)

rf <- ranger::ranger(y ~ z + clay + map + rel, data = d_tr,
                     num.trees = 300L, seed = 1L)
pred_rf <- matrix(predict(rf, d_te)$predictions,
                  nrow = nrow(y_te), ncol = length(depths))
score <- function(p, lbl) {
  c(model = lbl,
    rmse  = sprintf("%.3f", sqrt(mean((p - y_te)^2))),
    r2    = sprintf("%+.4f", 1 - sum((p - y_te)^2) /
                                 sum((y_te - mean(y_tr))^2)))
}

as.data.frame(rbind(
  score(pred_don, "DeepONet"),
  score(pred_fno, "FNO"),
  score(pred_rf,  "ranger (pointwise)")
), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
#>                model  rmse      r2
#> 1           DeepONet 0.500 +0.9842
#> 2                FNO 1.862 +0.7809
#> 3 ranger (pointwise) 0.483 +0.9852

Two things to take from this table, both of which cut against the marketing version of “neural operators”.

The forest is not beaten on its home turf. Scored on the training depth grid, ranger is at least as accurate as the best operator model. That is the regime a pointwise regressor is built for, and 500 trees on three covariates is a genuinely strong baseline. Any claim that an operator model dominates here should be met with suspicion.

The FNO’s R backend is the weakest of the three, by design. It is a small spectral network trained by plain gradient descent so the pillar is inspectable and installs with no system dependencies (§7). It is a reference implementation, not a competitive one, and the gap you see is the cost of that choice — not a property of Fourier neural operators.

The next section scores the thing that actually distinguishes an operator model, and there the ordering changes.

6. The property a pointwise model cannot have

Ask every model for the profile at depths that appear nowhere in training. The operator models accept the query directly. The random forest must extrapolate along a feature it only ever saw at 24 discrete values.

z_new <- c(7.5, 33, 61, 97, 133)          # deliberately between nodes

truth_new <- t(apply(x_te, 1L, profile_of, z = z_new))

don_new <- predict(don, x_te, newdepths = z_new)

d_new <- data.frame(
  z    = rep(z_new, each = nrow(x_te)),
  clay = rep(x_te[, "clay"],   times = length(z_new)),
  map  = rep(x_te[, "map"],    times = length(z_new)),
  rel  = rep(x_te[, "relief"], times = length(z_new))
)
rf_new <- matrix(predict(rf, d_new)$predictions,
                 nrow = nrow(x_te), ncol = length(z_new))

c(deeponet_offgrid_rmse = sqrt(mean((don_new - truth_new)^2)),
  ranger_offgrid_rmse   = sqrt(mean((rf_new  - truth_new)^2)))
#> deeponet_offgrid_rmse   ranger_offgrid_rmse 
#>             0.4718407             0.6636600

The ordering reverses. On the training grid the forest was ahead; asked for depths it never saw, it is not — because a tree can only return values it has averaged from training leaves, and its splits on z partition the 24 observed depths into steps. The DeepONet trunk, by contrast, is a continuous function of zz: querying it at 61 cm is the same operation as querying it at a training depth.

This is the claim Pillar 8 actually makes. Not “neural operators beat random forests” — §5 shows they need not, even on data generated by a smooth operator. The claim is that the operator model has learned a function of depth and can be interrogated anywhere on the interval, which is what you need to produce GlobalSoilMap-style standard depth intervals from profiles sampled on irregular horizons.

7. Backends

Both fitters ship a dependency-free pure-R backend (used throughout this vignette, so it knits offline) and a torch backend with full autograd:

fno_t <- no_fno_fit(depths, y_tr, cube(x_tr),
                    backend = "torch", device = "cpu",  # or "mps" / "cuda"
                    n_modes = 8L, width = 32L, n_blocks = 3L,
                    epochs = 500L, lr = 1e-3, seed = 1L)

The R backend exists so the pillar is inspectable and installable anywhere; the torch backend exists so it scales. They are not expected to produce identical numbers — different optimisers, different initialisations — and the test suite asserts agreement in behaviour, not in digits.

8. Limitations

  • The demonstration operator is analytic and noise is mild. Real depth functions carry horizon discontinuities, which a spectrally truncated FNO will deliberately smooth over.
  • Both models assume every profile shares one depth grid. Ragged horizon data must be splined onto a common support first — see vignette("pilar2-piml-profile").
  • The R backend trains a small network with plain gradient descent. It is a reference implementation, not a competitive one; use backend = "torch" for anything at scale.
  • Off-grid accuracy is bounded by the smoothness of the true operator. Neither architecture invents information between sampled depths.

References

Chen, Tianping, and Hong Chen. 1995. “Universal Approximation to Nonlinear Operators by Neural Networks with Arbitrary Activation Functions and Its Application to Dynamical Systems.” IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks 6 (4): 911–17. https://doi.org/10.1109/72.392253.
Kovachki, Nikola, Zongyi Li, Burigede Liu, et al. 2023. “Neural Operator: Learning Maps Between Function Spaces with Applications to PDEs.” Journal of Machine Learning Research 24 (89): 1–97.
Li, Zongyi, Nikola Kovachki, Kamyar Azizzadenesheli, et al. 2021. “Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations.” International Conference on Learning Representations.
Lu, Lu, Pengzhan Jin, Guofei Pang, Zhongqiang Zhang, and George Em Karniadakis. 2021. “Learning Nonlinear Operators via DeepONet Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem of Operators.” Nature Machine Intelligence 3 (3): 218–29. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-021-00302-5.
